articles.text: Henry Ward Beecher says, he "will write a book on theology and then die." Why not reverse his program and give us something reliable.
articles.summary: Editorial quip about Henry Ward Beecher's plan to write a book on theology.

articles.text: Riel says that Clark of the Hudson Bay company is responsible for all the muss and that he can prove that he has not done anything bad, but expects to be hanged. He devotes all his time to fasting and prayer.
articles.summary: Note on Louis Riel's claims after his capture.

articles.text: Matters are begining to look serious on the southern border of Kansas. There is every indication that the Texas cattle men are bound to make the drive as usual, and if the quarantine is made too strict there will undoubtedly be trouble.
articles.summary: Warns of trouble on the Kansas border if the quarantine against Texas cattle drives is too strict.

articles.text: The Illinois legislature has finally vindicated itself by the re-election of General John A. Logan to the United States Senate. This has been one of the most remarkable contests on recored, and the election of Gen'l Logan to represent his State in the senate is a welcome one to the State at large, as well as a just tribute to the honest statesmanship of the victor.
articles.summary: Welcomes the re-election of John A. Logan to the U.S. Senate by the Illinois legislature.

articles.text: They are trying to take a census of Dakota, but it will be wholly unreliable, as two and a half cents per name is all that is allowed the census taker for his work. Billings county is about 25 miles by 150 miles, and contains about 500 people. The compensation is inadequate to the service rendered.
articles.summary: Says the Dakota census will be unreliable because takers are paid 2.5 cents a name; Billings county has about 500 people.

articles.text: A wild wierd tale of a "feminine cow boy" riding an "Indian Montana thoroughbred pony" comes up from Sanborn and is quoted in the Mandan Pioneer as going to show that the cow-girl is a treasure. Now if Bro. Tuttle will rise up and explain what kind of a beast an "Indian Montana thoroughbred pony" is we will be truly thankful.
articles.summary: Pokes fun at a Mandan Pioneer story about a cow-girl on an "Indian Montana thoroughbred pony."

articles.text: At last Riel is captured and the Dominion government is wondering, now that he is a prisoner, what on earth to do with him. He will undoubtedly be tried for treason and if he is executed, the entire French population will be dangerously disaffected. If he is not executed, the rest of Canada will be as displeased. It looks now as though the Dominion officials want to compromise matters by declaring him insane.
articles.summary: Comments on the capture of Louis Riel and Canada's dilemma over his fate.

articles.headline: Come up to the Rack!
articles.text:
The Black Hills papers have come to the sensible conclusion that the Cow Boy was right in stating that it is entirely the fault of the Black Hills merchants that they have not had railroad connections ere this. But their way of acknowledging it, outside of the Spearfish Register, shows a want of backbone which is a lamentable characteristic of Black Hills journalism when speaking on public topics. It would be far better if the exact facts were spread before the attention of the Hills merchants and let them thoroughly understand that their treachery is known and give them a chance to do better in the future. Let them thoroughly understand that it is owing simply to them that the Hills is no better developed. Let them learn that they may make a better use of strangers than to play them for suckers. That their breaking faith with outside parties and making promises that they never intend to keep is a boomerang that has again and again reacted on the Hills merchants and should now knock a little sense into them. In fact, the Hills papers should read the riot act to their readers. Not cover up or palliate a thing, but show the facts in all their nakedness and teach the merchants how to do right instead of how to cover up their crookedness.

This article is prompted almost solely by the desire of the writer to see the Hills developed. We firmly believe that there is no extent of country of the same size in the world that has been so richly blessed with Nature's gifts as has the Black Hills.

This very development has, however, been thwarted and delayed, simply because of the back-capping of the Hills people.

It is time that all this was stopped. It is time that the Hills people should consider self less and the Hills at large more. This can be accomplished best by the Hills papers. Let them take for a text the fact that it is entirely owing to the treachery and broken promises of the Hills merchants that they have not now complete or convenient railroad connections.

Lest it may seem that we write this article because we did not have any more freight and express shipped via Medora, we will state that it made not a particle of difference from what point on the N. P. the goods were shipped. The amount forwarded from all point was to enter into the figures of the capitalists. The project of building the road is not yet given up but if it is brought to a successful conclusion it will be in spite of the treachery of the Hills merchant and not because of their aid and good-will.

We do dot mean to say that these remarks apply to all Hills merchants. There are a few bright exceptions to the rule but they are very few.

Now let us see if the Hills papers will have the courage to state the facts.
articles.summary: Editorial blaming Black Hills merchants' broken promises for the Hills' lack of railroad connections and challenging Hills papers to say so.

articles.text:

articles.text: A point that seems to have attracted but little attention in the Bad Lands is the subject of the laws on branding. Whether there are any in Dakota seems to be entirely unknown by our stockmen, all seeming to depend on the association rules on the subject. It is unfortunate however, that the headquarters of the association are in Montana and that the territorial laws which apply to the Montana association do not by any means apply to Dakota cattle. Our cowmen should see to it that laws relative to branding be passed in Dakota similar to those in force in Montana. As it now is all the cattlemen are members of the Montana association and governed by its laws while legally none of those laws apply here. This is a topic for discussion at the next meeting of the Little Missouri association.
articles.summary: Urges Dakota branding laws like Montana's, since Bad Lands cattlemen follow a Montana association whose laws do not legally apply here.

articles.text: As one means of ascertaining the condition of cattle in the country through which I pass I drop into the meat markets, where at a single glance, a long story is made short. At this place I found some of the finest beef upon the hooks I have seen anywhere in the south-west. Upon inquiry I learned that this meat was the product of alfalfa hay fed to steers that were quite thin in the fall. I saw the farmer who fed this lot of cattle, and found him much elated with his experiment. He paid an average of $25 per head and sold at an average of $60. This result from hay alone surprised me. To all appearance this meat is equal to a first class grade of corn-fed beef. Other farmers are following his example and hereafter this country will be blessed with an abundance of choice fat beef.—[Kansas City Record.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Kansas City Record on fattening thin steers with alfalfa hay.

articles.text:
R. G. Head, general manager of the Prairie cattle Co., has issued a circular containing the following, to his cowboys: "You can just as easily be a gentleman with leather leggings, snake hat band and big spurs on, as you could be were you dressed in broadcloth and linen. Politeness and gentlemanly manners cost less than most any cowboy's out fit. Yet you could come nearer estimating the value of an undeveloped quartz mine than you could these qualities; they are awful handy for even cowboys to have, especially when he goes to see his best girl. Do not deceive yourself by the delusion that if you can be connected with some six-shooter notoriety it will be a big thing for you. * * * * I will now call your attention to the most objectionable habit that is liable to find its way into cow camps—gambling—playing cards. * * * * You cannot play cards in camp during the working season and do your work properly at the same time. It will not be tolerated, and any employe knowingly violating this rule will be subject to discharge, and the strict attention of superintendents and foreman is called to this requirement. * * * * I am competent from experience to insert the suggestion that it will never hurt you to refuse a drink, neither will it stifle the good sense of the common community to fail to refuse to take a drink, provided you posess the manhood to refuse to repeat too often."

The above evinces the universal tendency of cowmen at the present time and the most of the rules apply to all cow camps. From this sentiment has also arisen a feeling among all cowboys to be gentlemen instead of toughs, and in our northern country it is scarcely necessary even to establish such laws.
articles.summary: Quotes R. G. Head's circular to Prairie Cattle Co. cowboys on manners, gambling and drink, and says northern cowboys already aim to be gentlemen.

articles.text: "Necktie Bill" Moore pulled out last Saturday with a load of freight for the Hills.
articles.summary: "Necktie Bill" Moore left with freight for the Black Hills.

articles.text: C. W. Sleeper is now in St. Paul. He intends entering into some branch of the cattle business.
articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper is in St. Paul and plans to enter the cattle business.

articles.text: Mrs. John Kiefer returned last night from her long visit east. Her health is almost entirely restored.
articles.summary: Mrs. John Kiefer returned from the east.

articles.text: Doc. Pennel pulled in Tuesday afternoon on his return trip from the Hills where he had been with freight.
articles.summary: Doc Pennel returned from freighting to the Hills.

articles.text: Almost all the outfits on the river have made their round-up preparations and will be ready to start May 25.
articles.summary: River outfits are ready to start the round-up May 25.

articles.text: F. D. Foster and family will arrive about the 25th. Mr. Foster will bring with him a full force of butchers.
articles.summary: F. D. Foster and family, with a force of butchers, expected about the 25th.

articles.text: C. W. Carpenter started down the river in a boat last Saturday. He will float down the Little and Big Missouris to St. Louis.
articles.summary: C. W. Carpenter left by boat to float down the Little and Big Missouri to St. Louis.

articles.text: T. K. Long, prosecuting attorney of Morton Co., was here Tuesday instructing our liquor men about the licence bonds.
articles.summary: Morton County prosecuting attorney T. K. Long instructed Medora liquor dealers on licence bonds.

articles.text: "All's well that ends well." The gorgeous hunting chariot has been turned into a refuse wagon for the slaughter-house.
articles.summary: The "hunting chariot" has been turned into a refuse wagon for the slaughter-house.

articles.text: As soon as the present work is completed, Medora will be spoken of as the model town for cleanliness on the line of the road.
articles.summary: Clean-up work will make Medora a model of cleanliness on the railroad line.

articles.text: W. A. Van Brunt, President of the Badger cattle company, arrived last evening from Milwaukee, Wis., and will spend about a month on the round-up.
articles.summary: Badger Cattle Co. president W. A. Van Brunt arrived for the round-up.

articles.text: Thomas Brophy, of Mingusville, brother to Mary and Annie, has been in town several days and expects to become a permanent resident of Medora.
articles.summary: Thomas Brophy of Mingusville plans to settle in Medora.

articles.text: The editor started for Chicago this morning and expects to be absent about two weeks. During his absence Messrs. Fisher and Levi Deffebach take charge.
articles.summary: Editor A. T. Packard left for Chicago for about two weeks; Fisher and Levi Deffebach in charge.

articles.text: The work on the new hotel is completed. Everything was done in first-class shape by Peter Book and Arch Boyd will soon have things in running order.
articles.summary: Peter Book completed the new hotel, which Arch Boyd will open.

articles.text: Come to think of it, we don't see any reason why the recent marriage should cause surprise after such an evidence of affection as was displayed in Truscott's foot-gear at a recent dance.
articles.summary: Joke about J. L. Truscott's marriage and his footwear at a recent dance.

articles.text: The entire stage outfit rolled in Tuesday evening, horses, coaches, station furniture and all. It is altogether likely, however, that the line will be partially or wholly stocked again for carrying the mail.
articles.summary: The whole Medora–Black Hills stage outfit came in off the road; the line may be restocked to carry the mail.

articles.text: E. V. Smalley, editor of the Northwest, with a party of four will be in Medora about June 1. A day's stop will be made and photographs taken of the places of interest and the points the country in general written up.
articles.summary: E. V. Smalley of the Northwest magazine will visit Medora about June 1 to photograph and write up the country.

articles.text: The case in Glendive against the Marquis fell flat. It seems that parties who expected to get sheep from him on commission sued him on two counts for $20,000 and $17,000 respectively. No case at all was made out, the judge dismissing it almost before it had begun.
articles.summary: A Glendive suit against the Marquis de Morès over sheep commissions was dismissed.

articles.text: T. Martin sent the weather report for the last six months to Gen. W. B. Hazen chief of the weather bureau at Washington and received an autograph letter in return complimenting Mr. Martin highly on the report and stating that blanks would be sent him and his name added to the volunteer contributors to the weather bureau.
articles.summary: T. Martin's six-month weather report won praise from Gen. W. B. Hazen and a place among weather bureau volunteers.

articles.text: The new contractor, H. N. Warren, who has secured the mail contract, between Medora and Deadwood should be made to either sub-let it, or put on the service needed. The route has become one of importance to the Hills and the northwest by the excellent stage accomodations given us by the Marquis DeMores, who would have kept it up had the contract for carrying the mail been given him. We learn that there are prominent stage men in this city who will at once revive the route and equip it with good horses and comfortable vehicles providing the contract for carrying the mail can be obtained at a reasonable compensation.—[B. H. Pioneer.
articles.summary: Black Hills Pioneer item: mail contractor H. N. Warren should sublet or run the Medora–Deadwood route, which the Marquis would have kept up had he got the contract.

articles.text:
MARRIED.—On the morning of the 16th., at Bismarck, by the Rev. Father ——, Miss Margaret, daughter of Joseph Gardient of New Richland, Minn. to J. L. Truscott, of Medora, D. T.

The above announcement is certainly a surprise to many here, but it would be hard to find a better mated couple or a couple who are so universally liked. After the first surprise was over, every one began congratulating and the best wishes of all follow Mr. and Mrs. Truscott. The former has returned to his ranch to prepare for the coming round-up work, while the latter has gone to her home in New Richland, Minn., to improve her health, which was rather poor here.
articles.summary: J. L. Truscott of Medora married Margaret Gardient of New Richland, Minn., at Bismarck on May 16.

articles.text: Again we repeat that if the saloon men would club together, we think it is possible to prevent Morton county from collecting license and the money can be left in our own county for school purposes. In any event several queer things have been done, showing that there may be some doubt as to the legality of the licence. If our informant is correct, fifteen dollars was demanded from the saloon-keepers of Belfield for license to apply before May 1. Three persons paid this, Max Bass refusing payment. That this fifteen dollars applied before May 1, seems evident from the fact that at least two of the saloon-keepers have not sold since May 1, and their money has not been returned. Here, the fifteen dollars paid was the first installment of the license money from May 1. In Belfield, Max Bass has not been compelled to pay, nor have those here who quit selling May 1. There are inconsistencies in these facts which go to show that there is some doubt as to the application of the law. Then again, why is it necessary and by what authority do the prosecuting attorney and deputy-sheriff of Morton county come here to collect the taxes? Why is it not the treasurer's duty to try and collect the license money first? Then in case of failure it is time for the prosecuting attorney to have warrants issued and send the deputy-sheriff to collect them. Then again, why is it that the checks for this money should be personal checks to T. K. Long? They were not issued to him as prosecuting attorney and even if they were, what other authority could receipt for this money outside of the treasurer of Morton county? These are a few points for our saloon men to decide immediately and before they pay another cent to Morton county. Then on top of all these, we think the law itself is unconstitutional. According to Mr. Long's statement Billings county does not owe Morton county a cent. All expenses incurred by unorganized counties are paid first by the senior county, in our case this is Morton county, and then by the territory levying a tax on the organized counties for the benefit of those that are unorganized. Then what earthly claim can Morton county have against Billings county? We do not cost her a cent and still are compelled to pay her enough yearly to keep a good school running here. This is a simple outrage and one that cannot be sanctioned by a constitutional law. By all means, we say to the saloon-keepers, have a test-case, show the unconstitutionality of the law and stop paying Morton county's expenses with money that should stay in our own county.
articles.summary: Editorial urging Billings county saloon-keepers to resist Morton county's liquor-license collections and bring a test case.
